response:
Diagnosis after generation 6 — the search has converged on a clear winner family and, importantly, on *why* it works. Two signals now carry all three forms of evidence: Inventory Overhang State At The Maturity Wall (fmb -3.49, alpha -3.7%, t=-3.97, Sharpe -0.27) and Receivables Lock-Up At The Maturity Wall (fmb -3.52, alpha -2.6%, t=-2.77, Sharpe -0.30). The state-versus-flow test was decisive: scaling inventory by sales and ranking it within the firm's own five-year history *improved* both the slope and the alpha over the raw-growth parent, which rules out the accrual/asset-growth interpretation and confirms the mechanism is genuine liquidity lock-up meeting rollover risk. Separately, the largest alphas in the archive still come from *stock* illiquidity legs against the same conditioner (peak-distance capacity -5.4%/t=-5.23; non-goodwill intangibles -4.4%/t=-3.99), but those carry no cross-sectional slope. With two generations left, this batch does three things: combines the two lock-up channels that each delivered t≈-3.5 slopes (S1), stress-tests the conditioner itself along two economically different definitions of rollover pressure (S2, S3), tests whether the flow-composition reading adds anything to the state reading (S5), fuses the best-slope and best-alpha investment legs (S6), and repairs the one working positive-side signal against its stated weakness (S4).

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Dual Lock-Up Overhang At The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), 5))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: Liquidity can be locked up in goods or in customer credit, and a firm sitting at the top of its own five-year range on both — with a large share of debt maturing within the year — has committed its entire operating liquidity to assets it cannot convert before the claims fall due.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The two channels have now been tested separately against the same conditioner and both produced slopes near -3.5 with negative alphas, and because receivables are measured here net of inventory the two ranked states are genuinely disjoint rather than double-counted. Scaling each by sales and ranking within firm history preserves the state construction that beat the growth-rate version, so this should compound the two effects rather than dilute either.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Overhang Against Pure Maturity Structure
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, dltt))))
HYPOTHESIS: What creates rollover pressure is the share of *borrowing* that must be repaid within the year, not the share of total liabilities: a firm whose debt is overwhelmingly short-dated faces a refinancing decision every twelve months, and if its inventory is simultaneously at an historic high relative to sales it will meet that decision without liquid resources.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The conditioner behind every large alpha in this archive is dlc/lt, whose denominator includes payables, accruals and deferred items, so the critic's standing concern that it partly proxies for total leverage has never been tested; replacing the denominator with total interest-bearing debt isolates maturity structure from leverage magnitude. If the alpha and slope survive, the mechanism is confirmed as refinancing timing rather than a leverage tilt, which is the single most valuable robustness result available before the final generations.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Overhang Against Cash Coverage Of Maturities
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, dlc))))
HYPOTHESIS: Rollover risk only binds when the firm cannot simply pay: a maturity wall is harmless for a firm holding cash in excess of what is due, so the fragility that interacts with inventory overhang is the shortfall of cash against near-term debt, not the size of that debt.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: This reformulates the conditioner as a coverage ratio rather than a share, which places every cash-rich firm at the benign end regardless of its debt structure — an economically sharper definition of the constraint than dlc/lt, and one that directly tests whether the mechanism runs through payment capacity. Together with S2 it decomposes the archive's workhorse conditioner into its two candidate economic contents, timing and coverage.
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Creditors Extending Duration To An Investing Firm
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)), RANK(SUB(GROWTH(dltt, 1), GROWTH(lt, 1))))
HYPOTHESIS: The resilience signal is creditors actively lengthening the funding of a firm that is still investing: long-term debt growing faster than the total claim stock means new money is arriving at long duration, an endorsement no management action can manufacture.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The archived positive signal (+3.6%, t=+3.04) risks collapsing into "capex by firms with little short-term debt" because its conditioner is dominated by a slow-moving level; replacing that with the growth wedge between long-term debt and total liabilities makes the conditioner a pure flow measure of duration extension, which is the mechanism actually claimed. This keeps the only working long-side construction in the archive while removing the quality-tilt confound.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Rotation From Cash Into Goods At The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(invt, 1), GROWTH(che, 1))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: The dangerous act is the conversion itself: a firm whose stock of goods grew while its cash balance shrank has transformed the one asset that repays debt into the one asset that cannot, and doing so ahead of a maturity wall is a self-inflicted liquidity squeeze.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Both the level state (inventory-to-sales position) and the raw flow (inventory growth) have been tested against this conditioner, but the *composition shift* between liquid and illiquid working capital has not, and it is the reading closest to the actual cash-management decision. If it underperforms the state version, we learn the effect is about the accumulated overhang rather than the year's rotation, which sharpens the final-generation specification.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Illiquid Balance Sheet And Inventory Overhang At The Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5), RATIO(SUB(intan, COALESCE(gdwl, 0)), at))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: A firm meets a maturity wall out of whatever it can convert; when both its working capital is jammed with unsold goods and its long-term asset base consists of unpledgeable operating intangibles, there is nothing on either side of the balance sheet to sell or post as security.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The archive has produced its strongest slopes from the working-capital overhang leg and its strongest alphas from the unpledgeable-asset stock leg, both against the same conditioner, but they measure different parts of the balance sheet and have never been combined — the short-term and long-term dimensions of asset illiquidity are complements, not substitutes. This is the most direct route to a signal that is simultaneously strong on the cross-sectional slope and on the FF5 alpha, which is exactly what the objective asks for.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---CRITIQUE Dual Lock-Up Overhang At The Maturity Wall---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: A defensible pooling of two separately-validated overhang channels against the same conditioner, with the receivables leg upgraded from growth to a within-firm state, but inventory-to-sales and non-cash-receivables-to-sales are strongly co-moving working-capital measures, so the "disjoint channels" claim is overstated and the likely outcome is a modest re-weighting rather than genuine compounding.

---CRITIQUE Overhang Against Pure Maturity Structure---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: This is the right diagnostic for the archive's most-used conditioner — swapping dlc/lt for dlc/(dlc+dltt) cleanly separates maturity structure from the leverage/payables content of the denominator — and the expression, sign and hypothesis are internally consistent; the only caveat is degenerate or missing values for firms with negligible total debt.

---CRITIQUE Overhang Against Cash Coverage Of Maturities---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: A genuine and economically sharper reformulation of the conditioner as payment capacity rather than debt share, complementary to S2 in decomposing the workhorse interaction, though che/dlc is unstable or undefined for near-zero short-term debt and coverage should be checked against the archived che/lct variant.

---CRITIQUE Creditors Extending Duration To An Investing Firm---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: The expected positive sign is hard to defend — the long leg is high capex *and* fast long-term debt issuance, and both the investment anomaly and the well-documented net-debt-issuance/external-financing anomaly predict *low* subsequent returns for exactly that cell — and GROWTH(dltt) explodes for firms with near-zero prior long-term debt, so the conditioner is as much a small-base artifact as a duration-extension measure.

---CRITIQUE Rotation From Cash Into Goods At The Maturity Wall---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is a close variant of the already-tested "Inventory Buildup Against A Maturity Wall" whose only change — subtracting cash growth — introduces a term far more volatile than the inventory leg it is meant to refine (cash balances routinely swing by multiples), so the composite will be dominated by cash-growth noise rather than by the claimed working-capital rotation.

---CRITIQUE Illiquid Balance Sheet And Inventory Overhang At The Wall---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: The two legs are presented as complements but are almost certainly negatively correlated in the cross-section — intangible-intensive firms (software, pharma, services) carry little inventory relative to sales — so SUMRANK will select middling firms on both dimensions and is more likely to dilute the strong inventory slope and the strong intangibles alpha than to combine them; a min-style or double-sort conditioning would test the stated "both jammed" mechanism far more faithfully.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Duration Extension And Earnings Cover For An Investing Firm
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)), RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, dltt)), 1)), RATIO(ib, lt))))
HYPOTHESIS: An investing firm is resilient when two conditions hold together: its debt mix is shifting toward long maturities, and its earnings actually cover the liability stock; that combination means the capital program is being funded patiently by creditors who can see the cash flow servicing it.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional
REASONING: The critique is well taken that long-term debt *growth* puts the long leg inside the external-financing anomaly and explodes off a small base, so the conditioner is rebuilt from a bounded maturity-mix change — the share of interest-bearing debt that is short-dated, differenced — which contains no issuance quantity at all. Adding earnings coverage to that mix change ensures the long leg is investing firms that can pay rather than firms merely holding little short-term debt, which was the collapse mode of the archived version.

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Liquid Reserve Shifting Into Goods At The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(che, ADD(che, invt)), 1))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: Within a firm's convertible resources, the split between cash and unsold goods determines whether a maturity can be met; a firm whose cash share of that pool has fallen sharply has rotated repayment capacity into product just as its debt comes due.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: Expressing the rotation as the change in a bounded share — cash divided by cash plus inventory, which lies in the unit interval — removes the unbounded cash-growth term the critic identified as noise-dominating while measuring exactly the same reallocation decision. Because it is a composition change rather than a level or a growth rate, it is also cleanly distinct from both the archived inventory-growth and inventory-overhang legs.

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Nothing Convertible Behind The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), at))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: When debt falls due the only assets that matter are those convertible within weeks — cash and receivables; a firm whose balance sheet holds few quick assets relative to its size, whatever the reason, must refinance or sell operating assets at a discount, and the market underprices that constraint.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: Fusing inventory overhang with intangible intensity would have combined two legs that are negatively correlated across industries, so instead this replaces them with the single balance-sheet-wide quantity both were proxying: the share of assets that are genuinely quick, current assets net of inventory. It subsumes the intangible-heavy and inventory-heavy cases in one coherent measure, keeps the conditioner that produced every large alpha in the archive, and uses only high-coverage annual items.
